title: String Similarity vs Semantic Similarity: Edit Distance, Embeddings & Meaning
h1: String Similarity vs Semantic Similarity: Edit Distance, Embeddings & Meaning
provisional_mission: Phân biệt hình thức và ngữ nghĩa
primary_entity_candidate: String Similarity vs Semantic Similarity: Edit Distance, Embeddings & Meaning

sections.heading: String Similarity vs Semantic Similarity: Edit Distance, Embeddings & Meaning
sections.evidence: String similarity and semantic similarity answer different questions.
paragraphs: String similarity and semantic similarity answer different questions.

String similarity compares observable representations: characters, tokens, q-grams or other symbolic sequences. Semantic similarity attempts to compare the meanings expressed by words, phrases, sentences, documents or concepts.
Levenshtein distance belongs to the first category. It measures the minimum edit cost required to transform one represented sequence into another.
It does not contain an intrinsic model of synonymy, negation, semantic roles, world knowledge, factual truth or real-world identity.
surface similarity ≠ semantic similarity

This distinction becomes especially important when text is normalized, transliterated, transformed into alternative Unicode characters or represented using learned embeddings. The representation determines what kind of similarity a comparison system can observe.

sections.heading: Begin With the Target Variable
sections.evidence: Before selecting a comparison algorithm, define what similar is intended to mean.
paragraphs: Before selecting a comparison algorithm, define what similar is intended to mean.

Question Primary comparison problem Are the strings exactly equal? Exact string equality Are they only a few typing edits apart? Edit distance Do they share the same words? Lexical overlap Do they discuss similar topics? Topical similarity Do they express similar meaning? Semantic similarity Does one statement imply the other? Entailment Do they make the same factual claim? Factual agreement Do they refer to the same real-world object? Entity resolution Should both satisfy the same search intent? Retrieval relevance
These targets overlap, but they are not interchangeable.

sections.heading: What String Similarity Measures
sections.evidence: String similarity operates on an observable symbolic representation.
paragraphs: String similarity operates on an observable symbolic representation.
For character-level comparison:
X = x₁x₂...xₘ Y = y₁y₂...yₙ
standard Levenshtein distance permits insertion, deletion and substitution.
The result has a precise interpretation:
The minimum number of unit insertions, deletions and substitutions required to transform one represented sequence into the other.
This precision is one of Levenshtein distance's major strengths.

sections.heading: String Distance Does Not Contain Meaning
sections.evidence: Consider:
paragraphs: Consider:
car automobile
These strings are orthographically distant while their meanings can be very close.
Now consider:
legal illegal
The strings are close, yet the prefix can substantially change the meaning.
At sentence level:
The patient has pneumonia. The patient does not have pneumonia.
Most of the surface form is identical, while the central proposition is reversed.
Therefore:
small edit distance does not imply small semantic change

sections.heading: Large String Distance Does Not Imply Large Semantic Difference
sections.evidence: The reverse implication also fails.
paragraphs: The reverse implication also fails.
physician doctor
have substantially different spellings while referring to closely related concepts.
Similarly:
The server stopped responding. The server became unresponsive.
can express nearly the same situation using very different lexical sequences.
large edit distance does not imply large semantic difference
There is therefore no universal monotonic conversion between Levenshtein distance and semantic similarity.

sections.heading: Identical Strings Can Still Have Different Meanings
sections.evidence: Even a string distance of zero does not establish semantic identity.
paragraphs: Even a string distance of zero does not establish semantic identity.
Consider the word:
bank
in:
She deposited money at the bank. They sat on the bank of the river.
The surface token is identical:
ED("bank", "bank") = 0
but context selects different lexical senses.
identical string ≠ identical meaning

sections.heading: Lexical Order Can Carry Meaning
sections.evidence: Consider:
paragraphs: Consider:
A dog chased a cat. A cat chased a dog.
The sentences contain almost the same words, but the semantic roles are reversed.
A pure bag-of-words representation can lose this distinction completely because both sentences contain the same token multiset.
This illustrates a broader principle:
information discarded by the representation cannot be recovered by the similarity function

sections.heading: Visual Similarity Is Another Separate Dimension
sections.evidence: String similarity and semantic similarity are not the only forms of resemblance. Unicode introduces a third useful dimension: visual presentation.
paragraphs: String similarity and semantic similarity are not the only forms of resemblance. Unicode introduces a third useful dimension: visual presentation.
Consider:
Hello 𝐇𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐨 𝑯𝒆𝒍𝒍𝒐 ℍ𝕖𝕝𝕝𝕠
A reader can recognize the same lexical content in each example, while the underlying Unicode sequences can be different.
This creates at least three distinct questions:
How similar do the strings look? How similar are their encoded sequences? How similar is the meaning they communicate?
These questions should not be collapsed into one score.

sections.heading: Styled Unicode Text Is a Useful Counterexample
sections.evidence: Presentation-oriented Unicode transformations can replace ordinary characters with alternative Unicode characters.
paragraphs: Presentation-oriented Unicode transformations can replace ordinary characters with alternative Unicode characters.
ABC ↓ 𝐀𝐁𝐂
This is different from merely applying a CSS font. The transformed representation can contain different Unicode code points.
At code-point level, Levenshtein distance can therefore report several substitutions even though a human reader recognizes essentially the same letters.
sequence difference: potentially large human-recognized lexical content: closely related
This is not a failure of Levenshtein distance. It is evidence that sequence distance and visual or semantic interpretation are different target variables.
See Styled Unicode Text .

sections.heading: Transformation Changes the Comparison Space
sections.evidence: Let T be a transformation applied before string comparison.
paragraphs: Let T be a transformation applied before string comparison.
dT(x,y) = ED( T(x), T(y) )
The resulting distance describes the transformed representations, not necessarily the raw inputs.
Examples include canonical normalization, compatibility normalization, case folding, transliteration and presentation-oriented Unicode mappings.
If:
x ≠ y but T(x) = T(y)
then:
dT(x,y) = 0
even though the source strings were distinct.
See Unicode Text Transformations .

sections.heading: Unicode Normalization Is Not Semantic Normalization
sections.evidence: Unicode normalization establishes standardized relationships between Unicode representations.
paragraphs: Unicode normalization establishes standardized relationships between Unicode representations.
It does not resolve synonymy, paraphrase, reference or meaning.
Unicode normalization → representation equivalence semantic representation → modeled meaning relationships
Similarly, transliteration changes representation between writing systems but does not itself translate meaning.
transliteration ≠ translation ≠ semantic similarity
See Text Normalization and Transliteration .

sections.heading: What Semantic Similarity Attempts to Measure
sections.evidence: Semantic similarity compares represented meaning rather than literal symbol sequences.
paragraphs: Semantic similarity compares represented meaning rather than literal symbol sequences.
The object of comparison can be a word, phrase, sentence, document or concept.
text ↓ semantic representation ↓ semantic comparison
Unlike classical Levenshtein distance, there is no single universal semantic representation or semantic distance.
Different systems can emphasize synonymy, topical similarity, paraphrase, retrieval relevance, semantic roles or other relations.

sections.heading: Semantic Similarity Is Not Semantic Equivalence
sections.evidence: Semantic similarity permits degrees.
paragraphs: Semantic similarity permits degrees.
Consider:
A: The company increased revenue by 20%. B: The company increased revenue.
The sentences are semantically similar, but they are not fully equivalent because the second omits the magnitude of the increase.
semantic similarity ≠ semantic equivalence

sections.heading: Semantic Similarity Is Not Entailment
sections.evidence: Similarity is usually treated as approximately symmetric.
paragraphs: Similarity is usually treated as approximately symmetric.
Entailment is directional.
A: A Labrador is running through the park. B: An animal is moving.
A can support B, but B does not establish that the animal is a Labrador or that it is in a park.
similarity(A,B) ≈ similarity(B,A) but entails(A,B) does not imply entails(B,A)

sections.heading: Semantic Similarity Is Not Contradiction Detection
sections.evidence: Two sentences can be semantically close because they concern the same entities and relation while disagreeing about the proposition.
paragraphs: Two sentences can be semantically close because they concern the same entities and relation while disagreeing about the proposition.
The contract expires tomorrow. The contract does not expire tomorrow.
Their lexical overlap is high and a generic embedding model can also represent them as close because much of their content is shared.
But they disagree on the central claim.
semantic proximity ≠ propositional agreement
Natural Language Inference models address relations such as entailment, contradiction and neutral separately.

sections.heading: Semantic Similarity Is Not Factual Truth
sections.evidence: A semantic model can determine that two statements discuss the same event or claim without knowing whether either statement is true.
paragraphs: A semantic model can determine that two statements discuss the same event or claim without knowing whether either statement is true.
semantic similarity ≠ factual verification semantic similarity ≠ truth
Factual verification requires evidence beyond similarity between representations.

sections.heading: Semantic Similarity Is Not Entity Identity
sections.evidence: Two records can contain extremely similar names while referring to different people.
paragraphs: Two records can contain extremely similar names while referring to different people.
Conversely, the same real-world entity can appear under aliases, transliterations, abbreviations or historical names that are lexically distant.
text similarity ≠ entity identity
Entity resolution requires additional evidence such as addresses, identifiers, dates, relationships or other attributes.
See Entity Resolution and Record Linkage .

sections.heading: Semantic Similarity Versus Semantic Relatedness
sections.evidence: Consider:
paragraphs: Consider:
car bus
and:
car gasoline
A car and a bus are conceptually similar because both are vehicles.
A car and gasoline are strongly related, but they are not the same kind of concept.
semantic similarity ≠ general semantic association
Distributional models can blur this boundary because words occurring in related contexts can become geometrically close even when their conceptual relationship is not synonym-like.

sections.heading: Symbolic Lexical Semantics
sections.evidence: One approach to semantic comparison uses explicit lexical knowledge structures.
paragraphs: One approach to semantic comparison uses explicit lexical knowledge structures.
WordNet organizes English lexical items into synonym sets and connects them through semantic relations.
surface word ↓ word sense ↓ concept / synset ↓ semantic graph ↓ concept comparison
This representation can capture distinctions that character edit distance cannot.
Its difficult step can be selecting the correct sense from context.

sections.heading: Distributional Semantics
sections.evidence: Distributional approaches infer semantic representations from patterns of language use.
paragraphs: Distributional approaches infer semantic representations from patterns of language use.
A word, sentence or document can be represented as a vector:
v(x) ∈ Rᵈ
and compared geometrically.
A common similarity function is cosine:
The vector should not be interpreted as “meaning itself.” It is a learned representation whose geometry depends on data, architecture and training objective.

sections.heading: Static Word Embeddings
sections.evidence: Static embedding systems assign one vector to each vocabulary item.
paragraphs: Static embedding systems assign one vector to each vocabulary item.
word ↓ fixed vector
Systems such as word2vec and GloVe demonstrated that words with very different spellings can become close in learned vector space when they occur in related linguistic contexts.
doctor physician
can therefore have low character similarity and high distributional similarity.
A limitation of a single static vector is polysemy:
bank
must represent financial, geographic and other senses simultaneously.

sections.heading: Contextual Representations
sections.evidence: Contextual language models produce representations conditioned on surrounding text.
paragraphs: Contextual language models produce representations conditioned on surrounding text.
token + context ↓ context-dependent representation
Thus:
bank loan
and:
river bank
can receive different contextual representations even though the surface token bank is identical.
BERT is an important example of this contextual representation approach.

sections.heading: Sentence Embeddings
sections.evidence: Token representations do not automatically provide an ideal sentence-level similarity space.
paragraphs: Token representations do not automatically provide an ideal sentence-level similarity space.
Sentence embedding systems instead attempt to encode a complete text into one vector:
sentence ↓ encoder ↓ fixed-dimensional vector
Sentence-BERT, for example, uses transformer-based encoders in a siamese/triplet architecture designed to produce sentence representations suitable for efficient semantic comparison.
Two texts can then be encoded independently:
u = f(sentence A) v = f(sentence B) similarity = cosine(u,v)

sections.heading: Bi-Encoders and Cross-Encoders Solve Different Retrieval Problems
sections.evidence: A bi-encoder embeds each text independently.
paragraphs: A bi-encoder embeds each text independently.
query ↓ vector document ↓ vector nearest-neighbor retrieval
Document vectors can be precomputed, making large-scale semantic retrieval practical.
A cross-encoder instead evaluates both texts jointly:
[query ; document] ↓ transformer ↓ pair score
Joint encoding permits richer pair-specific interactions but requires model evaluation for every candidate pair.
A common architecture therefore uses a fast retriever followed by a more expensive reranker.

sections.heading: Embedding Cosine Is Not a Probability
sections.evidence: Suppose:
paragraphs: Suppose:
This does not mean:
92% probability that the sentences mean the same thing
Score distributions are model-specific.
A threshold such as:
has no universal semantic interpretation across different encoders, datasets or tasks.

sections.heading: The Same Cosine Formula Can Measure Different Representations
sections.evidence: Consider:
paragraphs: Consider:
cosine(TF-IDF vectors) cosine(word embeddings) cosine(sentence embeddings) cosine(domain-specific embeddings)
The mathematical comparator can be identical while the representations contain very different information.
same similarity formula ≠ same similarity semantics
This parallels the same principle in string metrics: representation and comparator must be defined separately.

sections.heading: String Similarity Is More Directly Interpretable
sections.evidence: Under ordinary unit-cost Levenshtein distance:
paragraphs: Under ordinary unit-cost Levenshtein distance:
distance = 2
has a direct operational interpretation: two unit edits are necessary and sufficient.
A dense semantic score generally lacks such a simple decomposition.

Method Representation Typical interpretability Levenshtein Ordered sequence High: explicit edits Token overlap Sets or multisets High: shared lexical features TF-IDF Weighted sparse vector Moderate/high WordNet Lexical concept graph High: explicit relations Dense embedding Learned vector Lower Cross-encoder Joint learned representation Task-dependent

sections.heading: Semantic Models Do Not Make Surface Form Irrelevant
sections.evidence: Exact lexical information can remain decisive.
paragraphs: Exact lexical information can remain decisive.
Examples include:
A model that smooths all of these into broad semantic neighborhoods can lose information that matters to the application.
Rare identifiers, numbers, dates, product codes and exact names often require lexical or structured comparison in addition to semantic representations.

sections.heading: Semantic Models Do Not Automatically Fix Typos
sections.evidence: Typo robustness depends on tokenization, vocabulary, training data and model objective.
paragraphs: Typo robustness depends on tokenization, vocabulary, training data and model objective.
A misspelled rare term can break into unusual subword units and produce a degraded semantic representation.
An application can therefore use:
misspelled query ↓ edit-distance candidate generation ↓ corrected or alternative representation ↓ semantic retrieval
But automatic correction can also alter intent, particularly for proper nouns or uncommon identifiers.
A safer system can preserve both the original query and a high-confidence corrected form.

sections.heading: Hybrid Lexical and Semantic Retrieval
sections.evidence: Lexical and semantic retrieval solve complementary problems.
paragraphs: Lexical and semantic retrieval solve complementary problems.
query │ ├── lexical branch │ exact terms │ BM25 │ n-grams │ edit-distance candidates │ └── semantic branch dense embeddings semantic neighbors ↓ candidate union ↓ reranking
The lexical branch protects rare identifiers and spelling-sensitive information.
The semantic branch can retrieve synonyms, paraphrases and conceptually relevant text that shares little surface form with the query.
Neither representation universally dominates every retrieval task.

sections.heading: Do Not Combine Raw Scores Without Calibration
sections.evidence: BM25, normalized edit similarity, cosine similarity and cross-encoder scores occupy different numerical spaces.
paragraphs: BM25, normalized edit similarity, cosine similarity and cross-encoder scores occupy different numerical spaces.
0.8 edit similarity 0.8 embedding cosine 0.8 another model score
do not necessarily carry comparable meanings.
A hybrid system can instead use calibrated features, rank fusion or a task-specific learned reranker.

sections.heading: Cross-Lingual Meaning and Transliteration Are Different Problems
sections.evidence: Consider:
paragraphs: Consider:
good morning buenos días
Their character edit distance is large while their meanings can be close.
Cross-lingual semantic models attempt to represent meaning across languages.
Transliteration instead maps textual representation between writing systems.
transliteration = script / form mapping translation = language-to-language meaning transfer semantic similarity = comparison of represented meaning

sections.heading: Unicode Representation Still Matters to Semantic Models
sections.evidence: Semantic models do not eliminate lower-level text representation.
paragraphs: Semantic models do not eliminate lower-level text representation.
Before a model receives text, the application still performs operations such as decoding, normalization and tokenization.
raw Unicode text ↓ normalization / preprocessing ↓ tokenization ↓ semantic model
Malformed or inconsistent preprocessing can therefore affect embeddings just as it affects lexical comparison.
See Unicode and Grapheme-Safe Levenshtein Distance .

sections.heading: Unicode Transformation Makes the Representation Boundary Explicit
sections.evidence: Unicode text transformations provide a useful bridge between surface form and higher-level interpretation.
paragraphs: Unicode text transformations provide a useful bridge between surface form and higher-level interpretation.
source text ↓ Unicode transformation ↓ new sequence representation
The transformed string can differ substantially at code-point level while still being interpreted by a reader as closely related text.
For example:
Levenshtein 𝑳𝒆𝒗𝒆𝒏𝒔𝒉𝒕𝒆𝒊𝒏
A code-point-level edit metric sees different sequences.
A human can recognize the same lexical word.
A semantic system can also preserve related meaning despite the surface transformation, depending on its tokenizer and representation.
These are three different analyses of the same pair.
sequence relationship ↓ Levenshtein / string metric visual relationship ↓ rendering / glyph analysis meaning relationship ↓ semantic model
See Unicode Text Transformations .

sections.heading: Levenshtein Can Measure the Transformation Without Judging Its Meaning
sections.evidence: Let T(x) be a Unicode transformation.
paragraphs: Let T(x) be a Unicode transformation.
The sequence-level transformation distance can be written as:
dtransform(x) = ED( S(x), S(T(x)) )
where S defines the comparison sequence.
This value answers:
How much did the represented sequence change under this transformation?
It does not answer:
Did the meaning change? Does the output look attractive? Does it look similar? Is it easier to read? Does it refer to the same entity?
Those require different models or application evidence.

sections.heading: Styled Unicode Demonstrates Four Independent Layers
sections.evidence: A useful conceptual model is:
paragraphs: A useful conceptual model is:

1. SOURCE REPRESENTATION Hello 2. TRANSFORMED REPRESENTATION 𝐇𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐨 3. VISUAL INTERPRETATION recognizable styled form of "Hello" 4. SEMANTIC INTERPRETATION same intended lexical content in ordinary use
These layers are related but not identical.
A sequence metric should report sequence difference. A rendering system determines glyph appearance. A semantic system attempts to model meaning.
See Styled Unicode Text .

sections.heading: Semantic Similarity Still Does Not Guarantee Lexical Equivalence
sections.evidence: Even when two texts receive high semantic similarity, exact lexical differences may remain operationally important.
paragraphs: Even when two texts receive high semantic similarity, exact lexical differences may remain operationally important.
dose = 5 mg dose = 50 mg
A system should not discard the number mismatch merely because most of the sentence is semantically related.
A useful architecture can therefore preserve separate features:
{ edit_similarity, semantic_similarity, number_match, entity_match, date_match }
The application can then decide which differences dominate the final decision.

sections.heading: A Multi-Representation Comparison Architecture
sections.evidence: TEXT │ ┌───────────┼───────────┐ │ │ │ ↓ ↓ ↓ lexical semantic structured representation embedding features │ │ │ ↓ ↓ ↓ edit / overlap cosine / numbers scores model score dates entities │ │ │ └───────────┼───────────┘ ↓ task-specific decision
paragraphs: TEXT │ ┌───────────┼───────────┐ │ │ │ ↓ ↓ ↓ lexical semantic structured representation embedding features │ │ │ ↓ ↓ ↓ edit / overlap cosine / numbers scores model score dates entities │ │ │ └───────────┼───────────┘ ↓ task-specific decision
This architecture avoids forcing spelling, meaning, factual details and identity into one scalar representation.

sections.heading: String Similarity and Semantic Similarity Form Different Geometries
sections.evidence: Levenshtein distance creates a neighborhood based on edit operations.
paragraphs: Levenshtein distance creates a neighborhood based on edit operations.
small edit neighborhood = strings reachable by few edits
Semantic representations create neighborhoods based on the relationships learned or encoded by the semantic model.
semantic neighborhood = items close under the model's learned representation
These neighborhoods can intersect, but neither is a monotonic transformation of the other.
small Levenshtein distance ↛ high semantic similarity high semantic similarity ↛ small Levenshtein distance

sections.heading: A Practical Decision Process
sections.evidence: What difference matters? │ ├── sequence edits │ ↓ │ Levenshtein │ ├── token overlap │ ↓ │ lexical methods │ ├── meaning │ ↓ │ semantic representation │ ├── entailment │ ↓ │ inference model │ ├── visual resemblance │ ↓ │ visual / confusable analysis │ └── real-world identity ↓ entity resolution
paragraphs: What difference matters? │ ├── sequence edits │ ↓ │ Levenshtein │ ├── token overlap │ ↓ │ lexical methods │ ├── meaning │ ↓ │ semantic representation │ ├── entailment │ ↓ │ inference model │ ├── visual resemblance │ ↓ │ visual / confusable analysis │ └── real-world identity ↓ entity resolution
If an application needs several of these simultaneously, retain several signals rather than forcing them into one representation prematurely.

sections.heading: Relationship to Unicode Text Transformations
sections.evidence: Unicode text transformations make the distinction between representation and meaning especially concrete.
paragraphs: Unicode text transformations make the distinction between representation and meaning especially concrete.
A transformation can alter the underlying sequence:
ordinary text ↓ Unicode transformation ↓ different Unicode sequence
while preserving recognizable lexical content for a human reader.
This means a single pair of strings can simultaneously have:
non-zero edit distance high visual resemblance closely related intended lexical content
There is no contradiction. Each statement refers to a different representation or target variable.
Continue with Unicode Text Transformations and Styled Unicode Text .

sections.heading: Summary
sections.evidence: String similarity and semantic similarity are not competing implementations of one concept. They compare different representations and answer different questions.
paragraphs: String similarity and semantic similarity are not competing implementations of one concept. They compare different representations and answer different questions.

Levenshtein distance provides an explicit measure of surface sequence transformation through insertion, deletion and substitution. Its strength is precisely that its interpretation is narrow and well defined.

Semantic methods deliberately move beyond literal character sequences. Symbolic lexical resources, distributional vectors, contextual language models and sentence embeddings can identify semantic relationships that edit distance cannot observe.
But semantic similarity should not be interpreted automatically as equivalence, entailment, factual agreement, identity or truth.
Unicode transformations reinforce the same lesson. A string can change substantially as a sequence while remaining visually recognizable and preserving its intended lexical content.
Similarity is meaningful only relative to a representation and a task.
